articles.title: DAC vs AOC vs Optic: Picking the Right Short Link in the Rack
articles.excerpt: Most server-to-switch links in a data center are short — a metre or two from the server NIC to the top-of-rack switch — and there are three ways to make them: a direct attach copper cable (DAC), an ac…
articles.body: Most server-to-switch links in a data center are short — a metre or two from the server NIC to the top-of-rack switch — and there are three ways to make them: a direct attach copper cable (DAC), an active optical cable (AOC), or a transceiver (optic) plus a fiber patch cord at each end. They all carry the same bits at the same speed, and they fail in completely different ways. Pick the wrong one and you pay for it twice: once in the price, and again at 2 a.m. when the link is down and the diagnostic you need does not exist on the thing you installed. The three options, side by side A DAC is twinax copper cable with the connectors built in — no separate transceivers.
articles.author: Dheeraj Ramasahayam

articles.body: Why I built a godmother for women engineers 💛 Last Friday I spent one morning at Anthropic's Code with Claude: Women in AI Hackathon and built Madrina , a career coach in Slack for women software engineers. Madrina means godmother in Spanish: the woman who vouches for you. The idea started with a loss. A few weeks earlier, the Grace Hopper Celebration was cancelled 14 days before it opened . Eleven of my Slack teammates were set to go. For a lot of women, that week was the one time a year they got career advice from people who looked like them. The leak is after the hire 📉 We talk a lot about the pipeline.

articles.title: Proving AOS-8 remediation after CVE-2026-79868
articles.excerpt: Proving AOS-8 remediation after CVE-2026-79868 A patch ticket can close when a package installs. A vulnerability remediation record should close only when the organization can show that affected AOS-8…
articles.body: Proving AOS-8 remediation after CVE-2026-79868 A patch ticket can close when a package installs. A vulnerability remediation record should close only when the organization can show that affected AOS-8 systems run a fixed release and that adjacent untrusted networks cannot reach their management functions. CVE-2026-79868 needs both kinds of evidence because HPE describes an authentication bypass with administrative impact. The risk being closed HPE advisory HPESBNW05162 describes authentication bypasses in an affected AOS-8 interface. An unauthenticated adjacent attacker can gain administrative access, modify configurations and access or manipulate sensitive data, leading to complete system compromise. The CVSS 3.1 score is 9.6 with CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H .
articles.author: johnettagaweraks

articles.title: Erase unwanted objects from a photo for free: a 3-minute workflow (and where AI fails)
articles.excerpt: Every photo has that one thing: a stranger walking through the frame, a power line across the sky, a bin next to the front door. Erasing it used to mean twenty minutes with a clone stamp. AI "magic er…
articles.body: Every photo has that one thing: a stranger walking through the frame, a power line across the sky, a bin next to the front door. Erasing it used to mean twenty minutes with a clone stamp. AI "magic eraser" tools now do it in seconds, but they still fail in predictable ways. Here is how to get a clean result, and when the tool will let you down. What object removal actually does You paint a mask over the thing you want gone. The model then invents new pixels for that area, using everything around the mask as context. Nothing is "revealed" from behind the object; it is a plausible guess. That one fact explains almost every good and bad result. A 3-minute workflow I'll use the free Betatum object remover (disclosure: I work on Betatum). The same steps apply to any inpainting tool.
articles.author: Betatum AI

articles.title: I built a spam-check that reads your email like a tired filter would
articles.excerpt: InboxPrecheck is a paste-first checker for email before it goes out. You drop in a subject line and body, and it returns a scored pre-check: spam-trigger phrasing, format risks, CAN-SPAM structural ga…
articles.body: InboxPrecheck is a paste-first checker for email before it goes out. You drop in a subject line and body, and it returns a scored pre-check: spam-trigger phrasing, format risks, CAN-SPAM structural gaps, and the risky bits that make a tired inbox filter suspicious. I built it because most "why did this land in spam" questions are answerable by reading your own copy like a filter would — bored, literal, and quick to judge. Filters do not read, they score A content filter is not a person deciding your newsletter is evil. It tallies signals: all-caps.subject, "FREE!!!" density, link-to-text ratio, image-only bodies, a missing unsubscribe, a missing physical address. Most of those are countable. So the core of InboxPrecheck is a signal ledger, not a model guessing intent.

articles.title: An SSH honeypot on my own server: 24,000 sessions in five days and one very stubborn bot
articles.excerpt: I set up an SSH honeypot on my server: it pretends to be a defenceless Linux box, accepts almost any password and records everything done inside. There is no real system behind it. In the first five d…
articles.body: I set up an SSH honeypot on my server: it pretends to be a defenceless Linux box, accepts almost any password and records everything done inside. There is no real system behind it. In the first five days it received 24,218 sessions from 683 addresses, and almost nine in ten came from a single bot. I wanted to see attacks on my own server rather than in reports and textbooks: who shows up, what they type, and how one attack differs from another. Other companies' statistics answer "how many"; a honeypot shows "how". The setup The honeypot lives next to my portfolio site. It is Cowrie in an unprivileged, read-only container with every outbound connection blocked: whatever an attacker types, nothing leaves the box.

articles.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
articles.excerpt: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.
articles.body: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.
